svg.text: Origins of the Fundamental Rights (Constitution of India, 1950) — Indian-authored documents, 1895–1950
the law shall be equal to all
act only by virtue of law

text.tspan: Scope: Indian-authored documents; the Govt. of India Act 1935 is excluded. Every right also passed through the Advisory Committee (Vallabhbhai Patel) between the Sub-Committee and the Rau Draft; only distinctive links are shown. Arrows show the direction of derivation, from the older document toward the 1950

svg.text: text. Cell references use each document's own internal numbering; the column heading identifies the document. The Sapru Report 1945 (Tej Bahadur Sapru), chapter VII, states that ‘provision will have to be made for dividing them into justiciable and non-justiciable rights’ and refers the precise formulation to a
future committee of experts; the structure is built by the Fundamental Rights Sub-Committee in Parts I and II of its report.

text.tspan: Articles 12, 13 and 33–35, though part of the Constitution as adopted in 1950, are excluded because they define machinery rather than confer rights.

The Bill was drafted by the National Convention of 1924 under Tej Bahadur Sapru's chairmanship. Annie Besant chaired the sub-committee that amended it in 1925, and carried it to London for introduction in the House of Commons.

Article 22 has no antecedent in any Indian constitutional document: its rules on grounds of arrest, counsel and production before a magistrate had lived in the Code of Criminal Procedure 1898, a statute. The Sub-Committee’s s. 28 — its nearest forerunner — was deleted at the Advisory Committee on Alladi’s

svg.text: motion, and Ambedkar moved article 15-A entire in September 1949 to fill the gap the loss of ‘due process’ had left.

text.tspan: No antecedent clause states Article 17’s rule. The Nehru Report 1928 documents the intent — its narrative declares ‘untouchability is doomed’ and says its rights clauses ‘will go a long way to remove the disabilities from which these classes suffer’ — and the rule is first stated in Clause A of the Minorities

svg.text: Pact, Second Round Table Conference, November 1931, as quoted and endorsed by the Sapru Report 1945: the constitution ‘shall declare invalid any custom or usage… imposing… disability… on account of Untouchability’.
Compiled from the primary texts (Constituent Assembly Debates; digitised documents, constitutionofindia.net).
